title: The Ballplayer on the Corner
hook: A ballplayer on a Chicago corner heard his mother's hymns. *He stood up and walked.*
dateline: Billy Sunday · Born this week, on November 19, 1862 · near Ames, Iowa
summary: Billy Sunday, born November 19, 1862, was a Chicago ballplayer when a mission band sang his mother's hymns on a street corner.

story: One Sunday, after a round in a saloon, a few Chicago ballplayers sat down on a street corner downtown. One of them was a fast young outfielder for the Chicago White Stockings named Billy Sunday. He had been born near Ames, Iowa, 164 years ago this week, on November 19, 1862.

Across the street, a band from the Pacific Garden Mission struck up. He remembered “horns, flutes and slide trombones,” and voices singing “the gospel hymns that I used to hear my mother sing back in the log cabin in Iowa.” The year was 1886 or 1887; the accounts don't agree.

That log cabin had been a hard place. His father, a Union soldier, died of disease in an army camp in December 1862, about a month after Billy was born. The family was poor, and as a boy he and his older brother Ed were sent to soldiers' orphans' homes in Iowa. He grew up fast and ran faster, and in 1883 he made his debut for Chicago.

On the corner, the music did its work. In 1902 he wrote that he bowed his head and “the tears rolled down my cheeks like rivers of water.” Then he stood. “I arose and said to the boys, ‘I'm through. I am going to Jesus Christ. We've come to the parting of the ways,’ and I turned my back on them.” He walked to the mission and knelt. The next day at the ballpark, the team's star, Mike Kelly, told him, “Bill, I'm proud of you!”

He kept playing a few more seasons, married Nell Thompson in 1888, and in 1891 walked away from a $3,500 baseball contract to work for the Chicago YMCA for about $83 a month. In January 1896 he led his first revival of his own, in tiny Garner, Iowa. The Presbyterians ordained him in 1903.

Then the crowds came. Towns built him wooden tabernacles with sawdust on the floor, and walking forward at the end became “hitting the sawdust trail.” By the usual estimate about 100 million people heard him over his lifetime, and he claimed about a million came forward; both are reported figures, not audited ones. He hammered at liquor above all, and he helped build public support for the Prohibition amendment ratified in 1919.

He was not easy to admire in everything. Critics called him a sensationalist, and his income drew hard questions as the offerings grew. At home, his three sons struggled with broken marriages and money troubles while their parents were on the road; the eldest son, George, died in 1933 after a fall from a window. Billy Sunday died in Chicago on November 6, 1935.
The mission that sent its band out onto the street that day is still open in Chicago, still taking people in off the street.

quote.text: I arose and said to the boys, ‘I'm through. I am going to Jesus Christ. We've come to the parting of the ways,’ and I turned my back on them.
quote.source: Billy Sunday, in William T. Ellis, “Billy” Sunday, the Man and His Message (Philadelphia: John C. Winston, 1914), ch. IV “A Curbstone Recruit,” p. 41

scripture.text: And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
scripture.note: The prodigal's “he arose” echoes Sunday's own “I arose and said to the boys.”

why: The Pacific Garden Mission, whose street band Billy Sunday heard, still shelters people in Chicago, and its radio drama Unshackled! still tells stories of changed lives. God used a few musicians on a street corner to reach one ballplayer who had been drinking, and through him millions more.
prompt: Which song from my childhood still calls me back to God?
ask_yourself: Which song from my childhood still calls me back to God?
why_reel_line: A few street musicians reached one ballplayer, and the mission that sent them still opens its doors.
